## From iteration 3 (cand_0003) — the run kept spending iterations after the metric stopped being able to accept anything
- **Stop the run, or change the comparison, when the champion saturates the metric.** The gate is
`ACCEPT iff Δ̄ = mean_i(cand_i − parent_i) > 0.2·SE`, and the parent's per-task rewards are stored
rather than re-measured (`state.json`: `metric_calls = 80` over `iterations = 2` at `n_val = 40` ⇒
40 calls/iteration = the candidate alone). Once the champion holds `reward = 1.0` on **every** val
task — and per-task reward is capped at 1.0 — `cand_i − parent_i ≤ 0` for every task and every
candidate, so `Δ̄ ≤ 0 ≤ 0.2·SE` **always**. Iterations 3, 4 and 5 of this run are therefore
guaranteed rejections no matter what they contain. `budget.stop_at_reward` exists but defaults to
`0.0` (disabled). Suggestions, cheapest first: (a) default `stop_at_reward` to the metric's maximum
so a saturated run halts instead of burning three scoring passes; (b) tell the optimizer, in the
brief, the parent's **per-task** scores and whether the parent is re-measured, so it can compute
the reachable Δ itself rather than inferring it from `state.json` and prior-run reason strings;
(c) re-measure the parent in the same batch, which converts a saturated comparison from
"impossible" to "noise-limited" and lets a variance-reducing edit win.
- **A rejection at a saturated metric is indistinguishable from a regression, and the handover
format records it as one.** This run inherited "the single-cell `TypeError` fix regresses val —
never re-test" from prior `cand_0005`. That edit's real gate reason was
`paired Δ̄=-0.0250 <= 0.2·SE=0.0050 (SE=0.0250, n=40, resolvable effect size 2·SE=0.0500)`: the
move is **below its own 2·SE**, which `LEDGER.md` itself defines as `unresolved` and forbids
reasoning about as a regression — and it would have been rejected whatever it contained, because
its parent was already at 1.000. So a *correct* fix for a deterministic defect affecting 17.5% of
tasks got permanently blacklisted by two subsequent iterations. Suggest `rejected.jsonl` carry two
extra fields the optimizer is told to check: `resolvable` (`|Δ̄| > 2·SE`) and
`acceptance_was_reachable` (was `parent_val` below the metric maximum), and that the brief's
"already-refuted approaches" instruction say **an unresolvable rejection is not a refutation**.
Without that, every saturated run poisons its own search space.
- **The brief's breadth mandate and the REAL test contradict each other at the ceiling.** The
instructions demand "AS MANY real fixes as you can … a timid one- or two-edit iteration is an
under-used iteration", while the REAL test requires every kept edit to target a cluster *failing
in this iteration's trajectories*. At 40/40 those cannot both be satisfied, and the brief's own
focus line ("No actionable failures in focus") acknowledges the state without resolving the
tension. An optimizer reading the breadth mandate literally will manufacture speculative edits —
which the same brief names as the second way iterations get wasted, and which cost the prior run
three iterations. Suggest that when the focus block reports no actionable failures, the brief
explicitly authorise a **no-op candidate plus a written hand-back** as a valid, successful outcome
(it already does this for environment faults; the same clause is what is missing here).
- **Latent-but-passing defects have nowhere to go.** The two real defects I found this iteration (a
deterministic crash in the shipped verify snippet on single-cell ranges, 7/40; a missing
create-if-absent sheet idiom, 1/40) cost the agent a round each and are invisible to the score
because every val task has spare rounds. They are exactly the kind of fragility that plausibly
explains a val→test gap (prior run: val 1.000 vs sealed test 0.875), yet no part of the objective
can reward fixing them. Suggest a secondary, non-gating signal the optimizer is shown and can
optimise against — e.g. rounds consumed, or a count of tracebacks in agent/template-authored code
— so robustness work has a measurable home once correctness saturates.

## The step-3 verify snippet crashes on every single-cell `answer_position` (a defect in the capability text itself, found iteration 3)
- **What worked:** the *diagnosis* method — cross-tabulate a trace property against an **input**
property over all tasks at once, instead of reading traces. Tabulating "does `answer_position`
contain a part with no `:`" against "does the trace contain `TypeError: 'Cell' object is not
iterable`" over all 40 val tasks gives a **perfect 7/7 match, 0 false positives, 0 false
negatives**. That single table converted 9 scattered tracebacks into one deterministic defect
(7 tasks) plus two unrelated one-offs.
- **The defect, exactly.** `task_template.md:97` gives the agent
`cells = [c.coordinate for row in graded[RNG] for c in row]`. openpyxl's `Worksheet.__getitem__`
returns a **bare `Cell`** when the range names exactly one cell (`"B1"`, `"C14"`, `"'Calc'!B7"`)
and a tuple of row tuples for anything larger, so the double comprehension raises. The agent
copies the snippet verbatim — the tracebacks reproduce lines 97-98 character for character,
including `shown = cells if len(cells) <= 24 else cells[:12] + cells[-12:]` — so this is **the
capability's bug, not the agent's**. Affected val tasks: 31628, 46897, 51-12, 55979, 56563, 8942,
9726 (17.5%). All 7 recovered within one round and scored 1.0, so on val it is worth 0.000.
- **What didn't:** nothing new was tested. Prior-run `cand_0005` shipped the fix
(`rng_obj = graded[RNG]; cells = ([rng_obj.coordinate] if hasattr(rng_obj, "coordinate") else …`)
and was rejected — but see the next entry: that rejection does **not** show the fix is harmful.
- **Promising but not yet tried:** ship this fix in the first run that has val headroom, together
with a create-if-absent sheet idiom for the second latent defect (`answer_position` naming a
sheet the input lacks → `wb[name]` raises `KeyError`; seen on 402-43, which recovered). Both cost
the agent a round today, which is free only because every val task has rounds to spare.
## A rejection at a saturated metric carries NO information about the edit — and this run already mis-recorded one as a refutation
- **What worked (confirmed by reading the gate's own reason strings):** the gate is
`ACCEPT iff Δ̄ = mean_i(cand_i − parent_i) > 0.2·SE`, and the parent's per-task rewards are
**stored, never re-measured** (`state.json`: `metric_calls = 80` over `iterations = 2` at
`n_val = 40` ⇒ 40 calls/iteration = the candidate alone). So once the champion reaches per-task
1.0 everywhere, `Δ̄ ≤ 0` for **every possible candidate** and acceptance is arithmetically
impossible. **Check this before designing any edit** — two commands, and it can determine the
whole iteration.
- **The consequence that bites, and the concrete mistake it caused here.** At a saturated metric
every rejection *looks* like "your edit regressed", so a run accumulates false refutations. Prior
`cand_0005` (the single-cell fix above) is recorded in both earlier JOURNAL entries as refuted
hypothesis (a). Its actual reason string is
`paired Δ̄=-0.0250 <= 0.2·SE=0.0050 (SE=0.0250, n=40, resolvable effect size 2·SE=0.0500)` — the
move is **−0.025, below its own 2·SE = 0.050**, which is exactly what `LEDGER.md` calls
`unresolved` and says *"must not be reasoned about as a regression, in either direction"*. And it
would have been rejected whatever it contained, because its parent was already at 1.000. Correct
status: **unmeasurable, not refuted.** Same downgrade applies to prior `cand_0004` (−0.050 =
exactly 2·SE → "one task moved, cause unattributed", not "quote-stripping is harmful").
- **The generalizable rule:** before recording a rejected edit as refuted, check two things — was
`|Δ̄|` above `2·SE`, and **could the candidate have been accepted at all** given the parent's
score? If either answer is no, record it as *untested*, not as *refuted*. A false refutation is
more expensive than a failed experiment: it permanently removes a good edit from the search space
for every later iteration, and it is the one error an append-only handover cannot self-correct.
- **Promising but not yet tried:** when the parent is at the ceiling, state the arithmetic and ship
nothing. No prose lever exists; the binding constraint is the measurement, not the artifact.

## Iteration cand_0003 — NO capability edit: val is saturated at 40/40 so no edit can pass the REAL test, and the gate's own arithmetic makes ACCEPT impossible; shipping the evidence instead
- **Changes I made:** **none.** `prompt.md` and `task_template.md` are byte-identical to
`cand_0002`. This is a deliberate no-op candidate, not an oversight.
- **Why, verified from this iteration's own data (not inherited):**
1. **No failing cluster exists.** All 40 val tasks: `reward = 1.0`, all four metrics
(`soft_no_recalc`, `hard_no_recalc`, `soft_restriction`, `hard_restriction`) `= 1.0`,
`test_case_results = test_case_results_no_recalc = [1]`. Zero reward-0, zero partial-credit,
zero failing sub-case. The **REAL** test requires an edit to target a cluster *failing in
this iteration's trajectories*; no available edit qualifies.
2. **ACCEPT is arithmetically impossible, for this iteration and for 4 and 5.** The gate is
`Δ̄ = mean_i(cand_i − parent_i) > 0.2·SE` (verbatim from the gate's reason strings). The
parent is stored at 1.0 on all 40 tasks, per-task reward is capped at 1.0, and the parent is
**not re-measured** (`state.json`: `metric_calls = 80` over `iterations = 2` with `n_val = 40`
→ 40 calls/iteration = candidate only). So `cand_i − parent_i ≤ 0` ∀i ⇒ `Δ̄ ≤ 0 ≤ 0.2·SE`.
No prose can clear the bar. I checked this *before* designing any edit.
- **The one REAL latent defect I found, and why I still did not ship its fix.**
`task_template.md:97` hands the agent `cells = [c.coordinate for row in graded[RNG] for c in row]`.
openpyxl returns a bare `Cell` (not a tuple of row tuples) when `RNG` names one cell, so step 3
raises `TypeError: 'Cell' object is not iterable`. Cross-tabulating "`answer_position` has a part
with no `:`" against "trace contains that TypeError" over all 40 tasks is a **perfect 7/7 match,
0 false positives, 0 false negatives** — 31628, 46897, 51-12, 55979, 56563, 8942, 9726 crash
(`B1`, `I3`, `B6`, `'Calc'!B7`, `C14`, `'Overview'!B5`, `J2`); all 33 multi-cell tasks do not.
The tracebacks quote `task_template.md:97-98` character for character, so this is a defect in
**the text I own**, deterministic, on 17.5% of tasks. But all 7 tasks still **pass** (they had a
round to spare), so it recovers **0.000** on val and fails the REAL test — and prior-run
`cand_0005` shipped this *exact* code already (I read its diff in full).
Second latent defect, same verdict: `answer_position` naming a sheet absent from the input →
`wb["Sheet2"]` raises `KeyError` in step 1 (402-43: `TARGET SIZE: … across 1 sheet(s): Sheet2`
while the preview lists only `Sheet1`); `prompt.md:289` requires the sheet to exist in the output
but gives no create-if-absent idiom. 1/40, recovered, recovers 0.000.
- **Building on prior RESULTS.** Built on `cand_0002`'s ACCEPT (val 1.000, +0.050, broke nothing)
by changing none of it. **Did NOT re-try** the two edits prior RESULTs recorded as regressing:
the single-cell `TypeError` guard (prior `cand_0005`, 1.000 → 0.975) and the sheet-prefix
quote-stripping + `range_boundaries` advice (prior `cand_0004`, 1.000 → 0.950). Also did not
touch 53383's genuinely malformed prefix (`worksheet2'!C3:C6`) for the same reason.
- **A RECORDED REFUTATION THAT IS NOT ONE — read this before you write off cluster 1.** Both
earlier entries list the single-cell guard as refuted hypothesis (a). Its actual gate reason is
`paired Δ̄=-0.0250 <= 0.2·SE=0.0050 (SE=0.0250, n=40, resolvable effect size 2·SE=0.0500)` — the
move is **−0.025, BELOW its own 2·SE = 0.050**, which is precisely what `LEDGER.md` defines as
`unresolved` and says *"must not be reasoned about as a regression"*. And its rejection was
**inevitable regardless of content**, because its parent was already at 1.000. So that fix is
**unmeasurable on a saturated split, not refuted**, and it remains the highest-value known
improvement to this artifact. The same logic downgrades prior `cand_0004` (−0.050 = exactly 2·SE)
to "one task moved, cause unattributed". I did not re-propose either — re-proposal cannot pay off
when ACCEPT is impossible — but a future run **with headroom** should test cluster 1's fix first.
- **Refuted hypotheses (never re-test).** (a) `cand_0001`'s "val is capped, propose nothing" as a
*general* rule — `cand_0002`'s RESULT (+0.050, fixed 50768 + 59595) disproved it for a split
measuring 0.950. The correct form is narrower and is what I applied here: **only ship an edit
whose target task is currently, measurably failing** — which at 40/40 means ship nothing.
(b) Adding defensive code advice to an agent that is already passing: twice measured non-positive,
and in any case structurally unable to clear the bar now.
- **High-value clusters still NOT cracked.** On val: none — there is nothing left to crack. The
only real gap remains the **val→test gap** (prior run: val 1.000 vs sealed test 0.875, i.e. ~5

- **Plateau signal — this is a hard ceiling, not a plateau.** `cand_0001` +0.600, `cand_0002`

1.0. There is no lever to switch to: the issue is not that my edits are weak, it is that **the
measurement can no longer distinguish any two candidates**. Iterations 4 and 5 are in the
identical position; both will be rejected whatever they contain. The only way to generate signal

- **Focus next iteration.** Expect rejection and do not spend the iteration manufacturing a diff.
Re-run the two cheap checks first: (1) the per-task reward table — if a task has *dropped* off

## Iteration cand_0003
- **Strategy tried, and whether it moved val: establish the metric's own arithmetic BEFORE
designing anything.** Two commands — the per-task reward table over all 40 trajectories, and
`state.json`'s `metric_calls`/`iterations` — settled the iteration. The table shows 40/40 at
`reward = 1.0` on all four metrics with no partial credit anywhere (LEDGER rows 1-2: 0.950 →
1.000). `metric_calls = 80` over 2 iterations at `n_val = 40` proves the parent is scored **once
and stored, never re-measured**, and the gate's own reason strings give the rule
`ACCEPT iff Δ̄ = mean_i(cand_i − parent_i) > 0.2·SE`. With the parent pinned at 1.0 per task and
reward capped at 1.0, `Δ̄ ≤ 0` for every possible candidate. **ACCEPT is impossible, this
iteration and the next two.** Knowing that first changed the deliverable from "an edit" to "the
evidence", which is the only thing left that can carry value forward.
- **The generalizable process rule: diagnose the MEASUREMENT before the capability.** Every prior
entry in this file diagnoses the artifact. None asked whether the gate could still register a
win. That question is cheaper than reading a single trace and it strictly dominates: if the answer
is no, all downstream work is unscoreable. Recommend it as step 0 of every iteration, alongside
the per-task reward table.
- **A saturated metric manufactures false refutations, and this run had one.** At the ceiling every
rejection reads as "your edit regressed", so the handover fills with edits marked refuted that
were never actually tested. Prior `cand_0005` (the single-cell `TypeError` fix) is recorded as
refuted hypothesis (a) in both earlier JOURNAL entries; its real move was **−0.025 against its own
resolvable effect size of 2·SE = 0.050**, i.e. `unresolved` by LEDGER's definition, and it was
doomed regardless of content because its parent was at 1.000. **Before writing an edit off, check
whether the candidate could have been accepted at all.** A false refutation is worse than a failed
experiment — it removes a good edit from the search space permanently, and an append-only handover
cannot retract it, only annotate it (which is what I did).
- **What I got right by inheriting the *narrow* form of a predecessor's rule, not the broad one.**
`cand_0001` said "val is saturated, propose nothing"; `cand_0002` refuted that and was right to
(+0.050, two tasks fixed) because the premise came from a different run's score. The durable form
of the rule is neither of those: **only ship an edit whose target task is currently, measurably
failing.** At 0.950 that licensed `cand_0002`'s eight edits; at 1.000 it licenses nothing. Both
iterations were correct under one rule, applied to different data — which is what a handover
should transmit instead of a verdict.
- **Resisting the diff-producing reflex is a skill this run now has evidence for.** Three prior-run
rejections and this iteration all sit at the ceiling. I designed two edits (the single-cell guard,
a create-the-sheet idiom), ran them through the THREE TESTS, found both recover **0.000** on val,
and dropped both. Writing the designs down in PROCESS.md with their verification *and* their
blast-radius analysis means the next run with headroom can ship them in minutes — the work is not
lost, it is just not submittable here.
- **Subagents: correctly skipped.** The brief pushes fan-out per trajectory group. With zero failing
tasks the entire signal was two cross-tabulations over all 40 traces at once, and the decisive
evidence was a verbatim traceback line — exactly what a summarising layer destroys. Iteration 2
reached the same boundary from the other side (subagents paid off for *wide mechanical* blast-radius
audits). Combined rule for this benchmark: **fan out for breadth of audit, never for depth of
evidence.**
- **What to try next iteration (4 of 5).** Run step 0 first: (1) per-task reward table — if any task
has *dropped* below 1.0 it is a live failure, the REAL test is satisfiable again, and you should
diagnose and fix it; (2) `state.json` `metric_calls`/`iterations` + `best_val` — if the framework
begins re-measuring the parent, ties become winnable and cluster 1's fix (PROCESS.md, fully
designed and blast-radius-checked) is the first thing to ship. If both come back unchanged, ship
nothing and say so in one short entry; do not re-derive this analysis from scratch and do not
invent a cluster. The binding constraint for the rest of this run is the measurement, not the
prompt — that is a framework matter and is filed in `FRAMEWORK_IMPROVEMENTS.md`.

# Role
You are an expert spreadsheet engineer. You are given a question about an Excel workbook
and you deliver **a modified workbook file**, produced by running Python (openpyxl and
pandas are available) in a sandbox.
You are not asked to teach the user a formula. Most questions are phrased as "what formula
can I use to …", "could you suggest a formula", "how can I create an Excel 365 formula".
That phrasing describes the **result** the user wants to see in the cells. Your deliverable
is that result, already computed and stored as a value. Answering with a formula in the
cell delivers nothing that can be graded.
# How your work is graded — read this before writing any code
An automated grader opens your output file with
```python
openpyxl.load_workbook(output_path, data_only=True)
and compares, cell by cell, **every** cell of `answer_position` against a gold workbook.
It never opens Excel and **never recalculates anything**.
Three consequences decide almost every task:
1. **A formula in an answer cell scores zero.** `data_only=True` returns a cell's *cached*
value. A cell you set to `"=SUM(B2:B9)"` through openpyxl is saved with no cached
value, so the grader reads `None` and the cell is wrong — even when the formula logic
is perfect. The invariant you must satisfy is: *every graded answer cell holds a
literal value that `data_only=True` can read.* Compute the answer in Python and assign
the literal.
2. **Cells you were not asked to change are compared too.** For those the gold holds the
cell's **original input value**, so writing anything into them fails the task exactly
as hard as a wrong answer does.
3. **Python types must match** after the grader's normalisation (below). A date written as
the string `"12-Jun-16"` never matches a real date.
## The grader's value comparison, exactly
Both values are normalised, then compared with `==`, and **a type mismatch after
normalisation is an automatic fail**.
| Value you wrote | How the grader normalises it |
| `int`, `float`, `bool` | `round(float(v), 2)` |
| `str` that parses as a number (`"3.5"`) | `round(float(v), 2)` — so it matches `3.5` |
| `str` that does not parse as a number | compared **exactly**: case-sensitive and whitespace-sensitive |
| `datetime.datetime` / `date` | Excel serial day number, **rounded** to a whole day |
| `datetime.time` | the string `"HH:MM:SS"` |
| `None` | equal to `None` and to `""`, nothing else |
What follows from the table:
- **Do not round.** Write the exact computed number; the grader rounds both sides to 2
decimals. Rounding to 0 or 1 decimal yourself turns a correct answer into a wrong one.
- `3`, `3.0` and `"3"` are interchangeable, so int-vs-float is never a problem.
- **Where text is expected, keep the source text byte for byte** — same case, same
internal and trailing spaces. Do not strip it, title-case it, or parse it into a number
or a date. If the cell you are copying from holds the string `"25"`, copying the string
is safe; converting it to `25` is also safe; but converting a non-numeric label is a
guaranteed mismatch.
- **Where a date or time is expected, write a real `datetime`/`date`/`time` object**, not a
formatted string. Setting `number_format` changes only how Excel displays a cell; it
does not change the stored value the grader reads. For a date, carry **no time of day**:
the serial number is rounded to a whole day, so a stray `14:30` rounds the date up to the
next day and fails. Use `d.date()` or `datetime(y, m, d)` when the answer is a date.
- An Excel error string (`"#N/A"`, `"#NUM!"`, `"#VALUE!"`, `"#REF!"`, `"#DIV/0!"`) is
almost never the expected answer. If your computation yields one, the logic is wrong —
fix the logic instead of writing the error text into the cell.
## "Open at time T" means not yet closed at T
This applies when each record carries a **start** date (created / opened / hired / received)
and an **end** date (closed / resolved / completed / left, often blank for the live ones),
and the cell you are filling is labelled with a **single moment** — "open as of today",
"still open by the end of July", "outstanding at year end", "headcount at 31 Dec", "WIP at
month end". Count a record only if it had started by that moment and had not yet ended:
```python
open_at_T = start <= T and (end is None or end > T)   # an end date on or before T = closed at T

reading — "was open at some point during the period" — is a different and always-larger
quantity:
```python
open_during = start <= period_end and (end is None or end >= period_start)   # NOT the same count
Users routinely write the second while asking for the first: a predicate like "not closed
before the first day of the month and not created after the last day of the month" describes
the whole span, and it admits every record that closed mid-month — records that were *not*
open at month end. **When the quantity the cell's own label names is a moment, the moment
governs**, even where the instruction's own predicate describes a span; the span reading
makes the whole column come out uniformly too high, which is the most common way a counting
column fails. If the label genuinely names a window ("open during July", "active at any time
in Q3", "tickets touched in the month"), use `open_during`.

plain number of records that never ended. And across a row of columns labelled at increasing

record is still in your count for a moment that is *after* its end date, the rule is wrong.
